question: As reported in the press,1 the construction of a special waste-disposal plant has been authorised in the district of Santa Croce, in Teano (Caserta). The Council of State had previously issued two decisions ruling against the project going ahead and suspending work on it.

Building the plant would also appear to be in contravention of current EU legislation since it does not comply with the applicable objectives and existing regulations, especially in regard to key aspects such as contamination of soil, air and water resources, as well as damage to local flora and fauna.

Its close proximity to both a major archaeological and natural heritage site and a river means it infringes existing European legislation, in particular the Waste Framework Directive, the Habitats Directive and the Water Framework Directive, for a number of reasons. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.
Whether it is aware of this situation?

Given the criteria set out in EU legislation on the protection of natural environments and water resources and the prevention of pollution as well as the management of waste, including special waste, whether building this plant would be in compliance with EU rules?
What action it intends to take?
answer: 1. The Commission was not aware of this project. In the framework of infringement procedure INFR(2007)219 5 (2), Italy was condemned by the Court of Justice of the EU (3) to pay fines for failure to establish the infrastructure necessary for the treatment of the municipal waste generated in the Campania Region (4). This infringement does not cover special waste. 2.

Under the Waste Framework Directive (5), Member States must ensure that waste management is carried out without endangering human health and the environment. When waste is landfilled, the requirements of the Landfill Directiv e (6) must be strictly followed (7). Special waste such as hazardous waste can only be deposited in specific landfills for hazardous waste (8).

The disposal of waste in incinerators is regulated by the Industrial Emissions Directive (9). According to the Habitats Directive (10), any project likely to have a significant effect on a Natura 2000 site shall be subject to appropriate assessment of its implications in view of the site's conservation objectives.

Under the Water Framework Directive (11), Member States must protect and restore water bodies to reach good status. The Ambient Air Quality Directives (12) obliges Member States to keep the concentrations of some pollutants in the air below certain limit values (13). At this stage, the Commission has not enough information which would allow it to assess the compliance of the project with the applicable EU law (14).

3. Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, Member States are primarily responsible to ensure compliance with EU law, including verifying individual cases of potential breach of the relevant rules. In line with its strategic approach on enforcement action (15) the Commission focuses on systemic non-compliance.
